I've found comprehensive information about the "Lost in the Middle" paper by Liu et al. (2023). Here are the key findings:

## Overview

The researchers analyzed the performance of language models on two tasks that require identifying relevant information in their input contexts: multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval.

## Main Findings on Attention Patterns

Performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts, even for explicitly long-context models. The main discovery was that attention followed a U-shaped pattern where more importance was given to the beginning and end of the context window as opposed to the middle portion.

## Attention Mechanisms

Regarding the specific attention patterns, some "position-aware" attention heads are capable of capturing relevant information even when its position is shifted, and can capture important information across positions with attention patterns shifting as the position of relevant tokens changes, but other attention heads fail to capture relevant tokens and only attend to the beginning and end words, contributing to the "lost-in-the-middle" issue.

## Scope of the Problem

The pattern held consistently across multiple LLMs tested across different architectures and sizes.

The paper was published in 2023 and later appeared in the Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics in 2024.

## Overview of Transformer Layer Pruning Research

Post-training compression techniques have shown that transformer-based models can prune a significant number of parameters with only minor losses in downstream performance, creating efficiency gains at inference.

## Layer Importance Analysis Methods

Recent approaches have introduced diverse strategies and algorithms that analyze and quantify the relative importance of parameters throughout the network and prune layers accordingly. Different layers of an LLM play different functional roles, with earlier layers capturing local syntactic patterns and later layers responsible for high-level abstraction and reasoning.

## Types of Pruning Approaches

Pruning is mainly categorized into depth pruning and width pruning—depth pruning often removes entire transformer blocks, while width pruning trims hidden dimensions such as FFN channels or attention heads.

Layer-Wise Adaptive Pruning computes the relative importance of each decoder layer to decide which parameters to prune, and showed it is "extremely effective" in experiments on 32-layer LLaMA-3.1-8B model.

## Notable Recent Methods (2024-2025)

Reverse-order pruning is simple yet effective—simply pruning the last several layers performs better than many complex pruning metrics.

TrimLLM introduces a progressive layer dropping technique inspired by the layer-wise specialization phenomenon observed in LLMs, beginning with a thorough analysis of each transformer's layer contribution to the model's performance on domain-specific tasks.

LLM-Streamline has found that training a lightweight network to replace pruned parameters can mitigate performance loss, significantly outperforming existing methods.

I found comprehensive information about ShortGPT and layer pruning techniques for improving LLM inference efficiency. Here are the key findings:

### ShortGPT Overview

ShortGPT is a straightforward layer removal method that deletes certain layers in large language models (LLMs) based on a Block Influence (BI) score.

### Block Influence (BI) Metric

ShortGPT analyzes layer-wise redundancy through Block Influence, which measures hidden state transformations during LLM processing, and this metric is used to identify redundant layers for pruning rather than more complex methods. BI is measured by evaluating each layer's influence on the model's output, with layers scoring low on BI considered less important and suitable for pruning without significantly affecting performance.

### Methodology

The method collects hidden states of each layer during inference on calibration samples, calculates the BI score based on these hidden states, then sorts layers in ascending order by BI and deletes those with smaller importance.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Mixture of Depths and adaptive computation in transformers:

## Mixture-of-Depths (MoD)

Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) emphasizes how individual tokens pass through different numbers of layers, or blocks, through the depth of the transformer. Transformers can learn to dynamically allocate FLOPs (or compute) to specific positions in a sequence, optimising the allocation along the sequence for different layers across the model depth.

### How It Works

The method enforces a total compute budget by capping the number of tokens (k) that can participate in the self-attention and MLP computations at a given layer, with tokens to be processed determined by the network using a top-k routing mechanism. The mixture-of-depths method can be thought of as using the routing logic from MoE transformers, but rather than having multiple experts, MoD deploys a single expert which can be dynamically skipped.

### Performance Benefits

An MoD transformer can improve upon vanilla transformers by as much as 1.5% on the final log probability training objective for equivalent training FLOPs, while taking an equivalent amount of wall-clock time to train. On the other hand, one can train an MoD transformer that achieves training loss parity with an isoFLOP optimal vanilla transformer, but which uses a fraction of the FLOPs (upwards of 50%) per forward pass.

### Key Distinction from Other Methods

In MoD, unlike in early-exit methods, a token can skip middle layers, then be updated via self-attention with tokens that have gone through all the middle layers. This flexibility allows non-monotonic skipping patterns, making it different from early exit approaches where computation stops permanently.

## Key Findings

All top open- and closed-weight LLMs tested exhibit significantly lower performance in multi-turn conversations than single-turn, with an average drop of 39% across six generation tasks.

## The "Lost in Conversation" Phenomenon

The lost in conversation phenomenon occurs when LLMs take a wrong turn in multi-turn conversation and get lost without recovering. Analysis of 200,000+ simulated conversations decomposes the performance degradation into two components: a minor loss in aptitude and a significant increase in unreliability.

## Root Causes

Four specific causes were identified: (1) LLMs prematurely propose full answer attempts, making assumptions about problem specifications that lead to confusion, (2) they overly rely on previous incorrect answer attempts leading to longer "bloated" answers, (3) LLMs overly adjust their answers based on the first and last turn of conversation (loss-of-middle-turns phenomenon), and (4) they produce overly verbose answers, which likely introduces assumptions that detract attention from user utterances.

## Research Methodology

The authors developed a simulation environment based on a "sharding" process that transforms existing high-quality single-turn instructions into smaller, atomic "shards" that collectively contain the same information as the original instruction.

The paper demonstrates that the performance degradation in multi-turn conversations is primarily driven by increased unreliability rather than a loss in model capability.

## Overview

LayerDrop is a form of structured dropout which has a regularization effect during training and allows for efficient pruning at inference time. It is possible to select sub-networks of any depth from one large network without having to finetune them and with limited impact on performance.

## How It Works

LayerDrop applies structured dropout directly to the Transformer layers, maintaining computational simplicity while achieving significant model compression. Unlike standard dropout that operates on individual weights, this approach differs from traditional dropout methods by targeting entire layers rather than individual neurons.

## Key Benefits

LayerDrop regularizes very deep Transformers and stabilizes their training, leading to state-of-the-art performance across a variety of benchmarks. Additionally, small and efficient models of any depth can be extracted automatically at test time from a single large pre-trained model, without the need for finetuning. LayerDrop is as simple to implement as dropout.

## Experimental Results

Adding LayerDrop to a 16-layer Transformer improves the perplexity by 0.4, while adding LayerDrop to a 40-layer Transformer further improves the perplexity by 0.6.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about SkipNet and adaptive layer skipping in residual networks:

## Overview

SkipNet is a modified residual network that uses a gating network to selectively skip convolutional blocks based on the activations of the previous layer. It learns to skip convolutional layers on a per-input basis.

## Key Mechanism

The dynamic skipping problem is framed as a sequential decision problem in which the outputs of previous layers are used to decide whether to bypass the subsequent layer. During inference the most likely action is taken from the probability distribution encoded by each gate: the layer is skipped or executed.

## Training Approach

SkipNet formulates the dynamic skipping problem in the context of sequential decision making and proposes a hybrid learning algorithm that combines supervised learning and reinforcement learning to address the challenges of non-differentiable skipping decisions. The inherently discrete and therefore non-differentiable decision process creates unique challenges for how networks are trained.

## Performance

SkipNet reduces computation by 30-90% while preserving the accuracy of the original model on four benchmark datasets and outperforms the state-of-the-art dynamic networks and static compression methods.

## Conditional Computation

Instead of processing every input with the same computation, SkipNet learns when to bypass certain layers based on input complexity. This represents an important approach to conditional computation in neural networks.

## Key Findings

**Early vs. Later Layer Behavior:**

Attention heads in earlier blocks tend to focus on simple internal information (e.g., position), while attention heads in later blocks tend to focus on complex interactions between tokens (e.g., syntactic relations).

**Syntactic Structure Encoding:**

Research has found that specific attention heads in transformers are responsible for syntactic functions, while others capture long-term dependencies. Additionally, transformers encode syntactic tree structures in their representations, providing insight into how these models process linguistic information.

**Attention Head Specialization:**

Each attention head processes a segment of embeddings independently, capturing different syntactic and semantic relationships. Furthermore, one head may capture short-range syntactic links while another tracks broader semantic context.

Transformers inject positional information, typically through positional encodings or learned positional embeddings, so token order can affect the output.

**Evolution Across Layers:**

Attention patterns evolve across layers from syntactic to semantic to task-specific processing.

Based on the search results, here's what recent research shows about instruction following degradation in multi-turn LLM systems:

## Key Findings on Multi-Turn Performance Degradation

**Magnitude of Degradation:**
LLM performance drops significantly in multi-turn conversations, declining on average from ~90% (fully specified) to ~55% when tasks are presented in sharded form—a 39% decline across major models. Models like GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.5 Pro see just as severe multi-turn drops as smaller or open-weight models.

**Unreliability in Multi-Turn Settings:**
While aptitude drops modestly (~15%), unreliability more than doubles (+112%) in multi-turn responses. In multi-turn, the gap between a model's best and worst runs can exceed 50 points, meaning a single user session might swing from success to failure purely by chance.

**Mechanisms Behind Degradation:**
Multi-turn failure arises when task-defining information from the initial prompt becomes less accessible through direct attention. Multi-turn conversations show an average 39% performance drop, and LLMs often make assumptions in early turns and prematurely attempt to generate final solutions, on which they overly rely. When LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover.

**System Prompt Issues:**
The rule is applied in form but loses its substance through ceremonialization—the model follows the first few instances of a rule but by the tenth change writes "ran tests, passed" without actually doing so.

## Recent 2024-2025 Research

Recent papers from 2025 have advanced understanding of these phenomena significantly, with sharded simulation research showing that LLMs perform 39% worse and 112% less reliably in multi-turn settings, and studies documenting that instruction adherence degrades monotonically with turn count, with the strongest 2025 frontier models sustaining only around 18 reliable conversational turns.

## "The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers"

The paper studies how knowledge is stored in an LLM's weights via layer pruning: if removing a certain layer does not affect model performance in common question-answering benchmarks, then the weights in that layer are not necessary for storing the knowledge needed to answer those questions.

**Methodology:** The researchers identify the optimal block of layers to prune by considering similarity across layers; then, to "heal" the damage, they perform a small amount of finetuning. They use parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods, specifically quantization and Low Rank Adapters (QLoRA), such that each experiment can be performed on a single 40GB A100 GPU.

**Key Findings:** They find minimal degradation of performance until after a large fraction (up to half) of the layers are removed for some common open-weight models.

**Implications:** From a scientific perspective, the robustness of these LLMs to the deletion of layers implies either that current pretraining methods are not properly leveraging the parameters in the deeper layers of the network or that the shallow layers play a critical role in storing knowledge.

The paper (arxiv 2403.17887) was published in March 2024 and has generated significant interest in the community regarding transformer model efficiency and layer redundancy.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the paper "Reassessing Layer Pruning in LLMs: New Insights and Methods" (arXiv:2411.15558):

## Overview

The paper addresses how large language models' considerable scale necessitates substantial computational resources, and layer pruning is presented as a simple yet effective compression method that removes layers directly to reduce computational overhead.

## Key Research Questions

The paper investigates what the best practices for layer pruning in LLMs are, whether sophisticated layer selection metrics are truly effective, and whether the LoRA (Low-Rank Approximation) family meets expectations when applied to post-pruning fine-tuning.

## Main Findings and Methods

To answer these questions, the authors conducted thousands of GPU hours of benchmarking on layer pruning in LLMs across multiple dimensions.

The results demonstrate that a simple approach—pruning the final 25% of layers followed by fine-tuning the lm_head and the remaining last three layers—yields remarkably strong performance.

Following this approach, they pruned Llama-3.1-8B-It and obtained a model that outperforms many popular LLMs of similar size, such as ChatGLM2-6B, Vicuna-7B-v1.5, Qwen1.5-7B and Baichuan2-7B.

The authors released the optimal model weights on Huggingface, and the code is available on GitHub.

The paper was submitted on November 23, 2024.

## Key Findings

Confident Adaptive Language Modeling (CALM) is a framework for dynamically allocating different amounts of compute per input and generation timestep. CALM applied confidence-based early exit to encoder-decoder T5 models and showed 2–3x speedup on translation.

### How CALM Works

CALM introduces a framework that modulates the depth of computation based on the confidence level associated with each token's generation, allowing early exit from the computation pipeline for tokens predicted with high confidence. Early exit decoding involves several challenges, such as: (1) what confidence measure to use; (2) connecting sequence-level constraints to local per-token exit decisions; and (3) attending back to missing hidden representations due to early exits in previous tokens.

More recent approaches have built on this foundation. Saturation events provide strong support for early exit research, in which the final output prediction is consistently in the top-ranked prediction launched by the Feed-Forward Networks (FFN) in hidden layers, which motivated the CALM approach.

LayerSkip trains decoder-only models with early-exit loss from scratch using a layer dropout schedule. Shan et al. (2024) study early exit as a natural capability of pretrained LLMs without additional training.

Additionally, ADEPT (Adaptive Dynamic Early-exit Process for Transformers) is a novel approach designed to enable dynamic early exit in both the prefill and generation phases, with an adaptive token-level early-exit mechanism that adjusts computation dynamically based on token complexity.

## Recent Research on Gating in Transformers

GateSkip introduces a simple residual-stream gating mechanism that enables token-wise layer skipping in decoder-only language models. Each Attention/MLP branch is equipped with a sigmoid-linear gate that condenses the branch's output before it re-enters the residual stream.

Many recent works commonly apply gating, often to modulate the outputs of token-mixer components, though the function and impact of gating mechanisms remain insufficiently explored beyond their initial intuition.

## Gating for Attention Improvement

Gating can mitigate attention sink effects, with SDPA output gating effectively reducing massive activations and the attention sink, capping the influence that any single token can have on the Transformer's main information pathway, the residual stream.

When query-dependent sparse gating is applied at the SDPA output, models exhibit no attention sink and demonstrate superior performance in length generalization, achieving a gain of over 10 points on RULER.

## Layer Skipping and Gating Mechanisms

A regularization loss based on the mean and variance of gate values with adaptive coefficients helps control sparsity, where the mean term incentivizes smaller gate values and the variance term incentivizes a non-uniform distribution such that some gate values are zero.

These papers represent significant developments in understanding how learned gating mechanisms can improve transformer performance through better control of information flow in the residual stream.

## Paper Information

The paper "Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models" (arXiv:2404.02258) was authored by David Raposo, Sam Ritter, Blake Richards, Timothy Lillicrap, Peter Conway Humphreys, and Adam Santoro. The work is from Google DeepMind, and it was submitted on April 2, 2024.

## Core Contribution

The paper demonstrates that transformers can learn to dynamically allocate FLOPs (or compute) to specific positions in a sequence, optimising the allocation along the sequence for different layers across the model depth. 

The method enforces a total compute budget by capping the number of tokens (k) that can participate in the self-attention and MLP computations at a given layer, with the tokens to be processed determined by the network using a top-k routing mechanism.

## Key Technical Approach

Unlike Mixture of Experts (MoE), the approach chooses to either apply a computation to a token or pass it through a residual connection (remaining unchanged and saving compute), and applies this routing to both forward MLPs and multi-head attention.

## Paper Details

**Title:** The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers

**Authors:** Andrey Gromov, Kushal Tirumala, Hassan Shapourian, Paolo Glorioso, and Daniel A. Roberts

**Publication:** The paper was published at ICLR 2025

## Research Overview

## Overview

The Curse of Depth is a concept that highlights, explains, and addresses the recent observation in modern Large Language Models (LLMs) where nearly half of the layers are less effective than expected.

## The Problem

The Curse of Depth refers to the observed phenomenon where deeper layers in modern LLMs contribute significantly less to learning and representation compared to earlier layers. These deeper layers often exhibit remarkable robustness to pruning and perturbations, implying they fail to perform meaningful transformations. This behavior prevents these layers from effectively contributing to training and representation learning, resulting in resource inefficiency.

This phenomenon has been confirmed across the most popular families of LLMs such as Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, and Qwen.

## Root Cause

The underlying reason for the ineffectiveness of deep layers in LLMs is the widespread usage of Pre-Layer Normalization (Pre-LN). While Pre-LN stabilizes the training of Transformer LLMs, its output variance exponentially grows with the model depth, which undesirably causes the derivative of the deep Transformer blocks to be an identity matrix, and therefore barely contributes to the training.

## Proposed Solution

To resolve this training pitfall, LayerNorm Scaling (LNS) is proposed, which scales the variance of output of the layer normalization inversely by the square root of its depth. Across a wide range of model sizes (130M to 7B), experiments show that LNS consistently outperforms previous normalization and scaling techniques in enhancing LLM pre-training performance.

The research paper was published on arXiv in February 2025 by Wenfang Sun and colleagues.

## Paper Details

The paper is "Learning to Skip the Middle Layers of Transformers" (arXiv:2506.21103), authored by Tim Lawson and Laurence Aitchison.

## Key Concepts

The authors propose a gating mechanism that skips a variable number of Transformer blocks from the middle outward, dependent on the input token, allowing the allocation of fewer compute resources to 'simpler' inputs by skipping the middle layers, which are more likely to be redundant.

In particular, a learned gating mechanism determines whether to bypass a symmetric span of central blocks based on the input, and a gated attention mechanism prevents subsequent tokens from attending to skipped token positions.

## Results

At the scales investigated, the approach does not achieve improvements in the trade-off between validation cross-entropy and estimated FLOPs compared to dense baselines with fewer layers. This appears to be a negative result paper that provides valuable insights into what doesn't work for this type of architecture.

The authors release their code at https://github.com/tim-lawson/skip-middle

## Gated Attention for Large Language Models

The paper's central finding is that applying a head-specific sigmoid gate after the Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA) consistently improves performance. This modification also enhances training stability, tolerates larger learning rates, and improves scaling properties.

### Key Research Contributions

The authors performed a comprehensive comparison over 30 variants of 15B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models and 1.7B dense models trained on a 3.5 trillion token dataset.

### Two Main Mechanisms

The effectiveness is attributed to two key factors: (1) introducing non-linearity upon the low-rank mapping in the softmax attention, and (2) applying query-dependent sparse gating scores to modulate the SDPA output.

### Attention Sink Mitigation

Input-dependent, head-specific gating of the SDPA output introduces significant sparsity, thereby mitigating the attention sink, and sparsity in the SDPA outputs reduces massive activations within the model.

Sparse gating eliminates the attention sink, with layer 21 in the baseline model demonstrating a strong attention sink (83% on the first token), which is substantially reduced by the gate (4%).

### Residual Stream Benefits

By reducing massive activations, the model is less susceptible to numerical errors during BF16 training.

The paper has been accepted as a NeurIPS 2025 oral presentation and code is available on GitHub.

      - title: "When Attention Closes: How LLMs Lose the Thread in Multi-Turn Interaction"
        authors: "Dongre et al."
        venue: "arXiv 2025"
        year: 2025
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12922"
        role: foundation
        relevance: "提出 Goal Accessibility Ratio (GAR) 度量 attention 对 goal tokens 的可达性，发现多轮交互中 GAR 衰减。与 ThreadGate 研究的 GAR 衰减问题直接对应，是最相关的论文"
        abstract: "Proposes Goal Accessibility Ratio (GAR) measuring attention from generated tokens to task-defining goal tokens. Shows goal-defining tokens become less accessible through attention across turns while goal information may persist in residual representations. Layer encoding depth varies from layer 2 to 27 across architectures."

      - title: "LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation"
        authors: "Levy et al."
        venue: "arXiv 2025"
        year: 2025
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120"
        role: foundation
        relevance: "量化多轮对话性能衰减：平均下降 39%，不可靠性增加 112%。提供了 ThreadGate 要解决的问题的定量基准"
        abstract: "All top LLMs exhibit significantly lower performance in multi-turn vs single-turn, averaging 39% drop across six generation tasks. Decomposes degradation into minor aptitude loss and significant unreliability increase (+112%). Models prematurely propose answers and overly rely on previous incorrect attempts."

      - title: "Intent Mismatch Causes LLMs to Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation"
        authors: "Liu et al."
        venue: "arXiv 2026"
        year: 2026
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07338"
        role: context
        relevance: "认为多轮失败的根因是 intent alignment gap 而非模型能力不足，且 scaling 无法解决。为 ThreadGate 的架构级方案提供动机"
        abstract: "Argues that Lost in Conversation stems from an intent alignment gap rather than intrinsic capability deficits. Theoretically shows that scaling model size or improving training alone cannot resolve this gap, as it arises from structural ambiguity in conversational context."

      - title: "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts"
        authors: "Liu et al."
        venue: "TACL 2024"
        year: 2023
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172"
        role: foundation
        relevance: "发现 LLM 对长上下文呈 U 型 attention 分布（首尾强、中间弱）。ThreadGate 关注的多轮场景是此现象在 turn boundary 上的扩展"
        abstract: "Finds performance is highest when relevant information occurs at beginning or end of input context, significantly degrading for middle positions. Demonstrates U-shaped attention pattern across multiple LLM architectures. Some attention heads only attend to beginning and end."

      - title: "Style Amnesia: Investigating Speaking Style Degradation and Mitigation in Multi-Turn Spoken Language Models"
        authors: "Anonymous"
        venue: "arXiv 2025"
        year: 2025
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23578"
        role: context
        relevance: "报告多轮对话中 style instruction 遵循的衰减，system message 比 user message 更严重。体现多轮退化的另一个维度"
        abstract: "Investigates speaking style degradation in multi-turn spoken language models. Finds style instruction placed in system messages degrades more than in user messages, despite system messages being designed for persistent conversation-level instructions."

  residual_gating:
    description: "Gating mechanisms for transformer residual connections and adaptive depth"
    papers:
      - title: "Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models"
        authors: "Raposo et al."
        venue: "arXiv 2024 (Google DeepMind)"
        year: 2024
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02258"
        role: method-component
        relevance: "用 top-k routing 决定每层处理哪些 token，允许非单调 layer skipping。ThreadGate 的 turn-conditioned gating 可视为 MoD 在 turn boundary 上的特化"
        abstract: "Transformers learn to dynamically allocate FLOPs to specific sequence positions per layer via top-k routing. Tokens can skip middle layers then be updated via self-attention with tokens that went through all layers. Achieves 1.5% improvement in training loss or 50% FLOP reduction at parity."

      - title: "Confident Adaptive Language Modeling (CALM)"
        authors: "Schuster et al."
        venue: "NeurIPS 2022"
        year: 2022
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07061"
        role: method-component
        relevance: "基于置信度的 early exit 框架，每 token 动态分配计算深度。ThreadGate 的 gating 机制与 CALM 的 early exit 互补：CALM 是 monotonic exit，ThreadGate 允许 selective layer gating"
        abstract: "Framework for dynamically allocating different amounts of compute per input and generation timestep based on confidence. Achieves up to 3x speedup while provably maintaining high performance. Addresses challenges of confidence measures, sequence-level constraints, and attending to missing representations."

      - title: "Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free"
        authors: "Qiu et al."
        venue: "NeurIPS 2025 (Oral)"
        year: 2025
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708"
        role: method-component
        relevance: "在 SDPA 输出加 sigmoid gate 可消除 attention sink、提升稳定性。ThreadGate 的 gating 设计可参考其 head-specific sigmoid gate 机制"
        abstract: "Applies head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA output. Comprehensive comparison over 30 variants of 15B MoE and 1.7B dense models. Eliminates attention sink (83% to 4% on first token), improves training stability, and enhances scaling properties."

      - title: "SkipNet: Learning Dynamic Routing in Convolutional Networks"
        authors: "Wang et al."
        venue: "ECCV 2018"
        year: 2018
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.09485"
        role: method-component
        relevance: "残差网络中用 gating network 逐层决定是否 skip，用 RL+SL 混合训练解决不可微问题。ThreadGate 的 per-layer gating 设计的先驱工作"
        abstract: "Uses gating network to selectively skip convolutional blocks based on previous layer activations. Frames dynamic skipping as sequential decision problem. Hybrid supervised+reinforcement learning for non-differentiable decisions. Reduces computation 30-90% while preserving accuracy."

      - title: "Adaptive Layer-skipping in Pre-trained LLMs (FlexiDepth)"
        authors: "Luo et al."
        venue: "arXiv 2025"
        year: 2025
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23798"
        role: direct-competitor
        relevance: "FlexiDepth 在预训练 LLM 上插入 plug-in router+adapter 实现自适应 layer skipping，不改原参数。与 ThreadGate 的冻结模型+gating 方案高度类似，是直接竞品"
        abstract: "FlexiDepth dynamically adjusts Transformer layers used during generation via plug-in router and adapter, without modifying original parameters. Applied to Llama-3-8B, skips 8/32 layers while maintaining full benchmark performance."

      - title: "Learning to Skip the Middle Layers of Transformers"
        authors: "Lawson et al."
        venue: "arXiv 2025"
        year: 2025
        url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21103"
        role: context
        relevance: "尝试 symmetric middle-out layer skipping + gated attention，但在其实验规模下未优于 dense baseline。提供了负面结果参考"
        abstract: "Proposes gating mechanism that skips variable number of middle Transformer blocks based on input token. At investigated scales, does not improve validation cross-entropy vs FLOPs trade-off compared to dense baselines with fewer layers. Valuable negative result."
